To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) there are a large number of published genetic association studies in the field of schizophrenia, (ii) there is a small number of genetic variants that have been replicated in independent samples, (iii) these variants are located in a large number of different genes, and (iv) the variants are involved in many different biological processes.

we have developed the first regularly updated online database for systematically synthesized and ranked evidence of genetic association for schizophrenia, and that this database currently contains 24 nominally significant associations in 16 genes.

the SzGene database contains a comprehensive collection of all genetic association studies published for schizophrenia, and that it provides systematic evidence of genetic associations with schizophrenia for 16 genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods and tools for systematic meta analyses in the field of psychiatric genetics and the application of these methods to the analysis of large-scale genetic data.
the development of new methods for the synthesis and meta analysis of data from genetic association studies in complex traits, and the application of these methods to schizophrenia.
the development and maintenance of a comprehensive online resource for the interpretation of genetic association studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic association findings in schizophrenia have so far not been very impressive.

there is no single genetic risk factor of major effect for schizophrenia, but that a large number of genetic variants with modest effect size are likely to contribute to the genetic susceptibility to this disorder.
there is currently no conclusive evidence for any genetic risk factor in schizophrenia, but there are a number of interesting candidates for which further replication efforts are warranted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although the evidence is not yet compelling, the results of our analyses do provide some initial support for the notion that genetic factors may play an etiological role in schizophrenia.
there is no single gene for schizophrenia, but that the disorder likely results from an interaction of several genetic variants of small to moderate effect sizes.
, while there is no evidence for a single major susceptibility locus for schizophrenia, a number of genetic variants with small effects may contribute to disease risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic architecture of schizophrenia is highly heterogeneous and that no single gene can account for a substantial proportion of the genetic risk.
the current evidence base for the genetic association of schizophrenia is not as weak as it has often been portrayed in the literature.
there is no clear evidence of any single genetic variant being associated with increased risk of schizophrenia.
